# Introduction

A table of p-values says little about how far it can be trusted. This vignette
goes through four checks that `r Biocpkg("exposomeSC")` makes easy, on the
example data of the package: airway epithelial cells of six heavy smokers and
six never smokers from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, which the main vignette
describes. The first two are run on basal cells only, to keep the vignette
short.

With 12 donors the checks cannot settle anything about the methods. They show
how each check is done and what it can and cannot tell.

# Installation

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("exposomeSC")
```

# The observed result

```{r data, message=FALSE}
library(exposomeSC)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
x <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "hlca_airway_subset.rds",
    package = "exposomeSC"))
```

```{r observed}
observed <- run_sc_exwas(x, exposure = "smoking", covariates = "chemistry_v3",
    celltypes = "Basal")
summarise <- function(fit) {
    data.frame(tests = nrow(fit), calls = sum(fit$padj_global < 0.05),
        p_below_0.05 = round(mean(fit$pvalue < 0.05), 3))
}
summarise(observed)
```

A call is a gene with `padj_global` below 0.05. With one cell type in the run,
`padj_global` is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment over the genes tested in
basal cells.

# Permuting the exposure among the donors {#permutation}

A permutation shuffles the smoking statuses among the donors and leaves the
counts and the covariates as they are. If smoking had no part in the counts,
the observed labelling would be one of many that were equally likely, and the
analysis of a shuffled labelling shows what the pipeline returns on these
counts in that case. A single shuffled labelling is not unrelated to the
observed one, though: some donors keep their own status, and a difference
between smokers and never smokers passes in part into the shuffled comparison.

The model adjusts for the 10x chemistry, and the status is permuted within
each chemistry, so that the two chemistries keep their numbers of smokers:

```{r design}
design <- exposureData(x)
table(smoking = design[, "smoking"], chemistry_v3 = design[, "chemistry_v3"])
choose(4, 2) * choose(8, 4)
```

There are 420 ways to label two of the four donors of one chemistry and four
of the eight donors of the other as smokers; the observed labelling is one of
them. A labelling and its mirror image, with every status reversed, give the
same tests, so these are 210 different analyses. Twenty labellings are drawn
here, each with a seed of its own.

```{r permutations}
permute_within <- function(values, strata) {
    for (level in unique(strata)) {
        rows <- which(strata == level)
        values[rows] <- values[rows][sample.int(length(rows))]
    }
    values
}
permuted_fit <- function(seed) {
    set.seed(seed)
    labels <- design
    labels[, "smoking"] <- permute_within(design[, "smoking"],
        design[, "chemistry_v3"])
    permuted <- x
    exposureData(permuted) <- labels
    fit <- run_sc_exwas(permuted, exposure = "smoking",
        covariates = "chemistry_v3", celltypes = "Basal")
    metadata(fit)$status <- labels[, "smoking"]
    fit
}
fits <- lapply(1:20, permuted_fit)
permutations <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, function(fit) {
    same_label <- sum(metadata(fit)$status == design[, "smoking"])
    cbind(same_label = same_label, summarise(fit))
}))
permutations
statuses <- t(vapply(fits, function(fit) metadata(fit)$status, numeric(12)))
mirrored <- statuses[, 1] == 0
statuses[mirrored, ] <- 1 - statuses[mirrored, ]
nrow(unique(statuses))
```

`same_label` is the number of donors whose permuted status is their own; the
observed labelling would have 12 and its mirror image 0, and
`r sum(permutations$same_label %in% c(0, 12))` of the twenty have either. The
last number counts the different analyses among the twenty, a labelling and
its mirror image taken as one: drawn each on its own, two could have been the
same. In
`r sum(permutations$calls > 0)` of the 20 permutations at least one gene was
called, and the fraction of p-values below 0.05 lay between
`r min(permutations$p_below_0.05)` and `r max(permutations$p_below_0.05)`,
with a mean of `r round(mean(permutations$p_below_0.05), 3)`; for the observed
status it is `r summarise(observed)$p_below_0.05`.

```{r histograms}
#| fig.cap: >-
#|   P-values of the genes tested in basal cells, for the observed smoking
#|   status and for the permutation with the most calls.
most <- which.max(permutations$calls)
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(observed$pvalue, breaks = 20, main = "Observed status",
    xlab = "p-value", col = "grey80", border = "white")
hist(fits[[most]]$pvalue, breaks = 20, main = paste("Permutation", most),
    xlab = "p-value", col = "grey80", border = "white")
par(old)
```

## Calls under a permuted status come together

The permutation with the most calls is worth a look:

```{r called}
called <- fits[[most]]$gene[fits[[most]]$padj_global < 0.05]
called <- sort(rowData(x)[called, "symbol"])
called
replication <- c("BIRC5", "CDC20", "MCM3", "MCM4", "MCM5", "TYMS")
```

The list was read after it was printed. Among its `r length(called)` genes are
`r length(intersect(replication, called))` genes of DNA replication and
mitosis: *BIRC5*, *CDC20*, *MCM3*, *MCM4*, *MCM5* and *TYMS*. Genes like these
are expressed together in dividing cells, so they rise and fall together from
donor to donor, and one difference between two groups of donors can bring many
of them below the threshold at once. *MKI67* and *TOP2A* are two usual markers
of dividing cells. The next lines say whether they were tested and whether
either was called, and count, for each donor, the sampled basal cells with a
count of either. A count of the called genes themselves would only say the
calls again.

```{r dividing}
markers <- rownames(x)[rowData(x)$symbol %in% c("MKI67", "TOP2A")]
markers %in% fits[[most]]$gene
intersect(c("MKI67", "TOP2A"), called)
basal_cells <- x[, x$cell_type == "Basal"]
with_marker <- Matrix::colSums(counts(basal_cells)[markers, ] > 0) > 0
status <- metadata(fits[[most]])$status
names(status) <- rownames(design)
by_donor <- tapply(with_marker, basal_cells$donor_id, sum)
data.frame(permuted_status = status[names(by_donor)],
    observed_status = design[names(by_donor), "smoking"],
    cells_with_marker = as.vector(by_donor),
    cells = as.vector(table(basal_cells$donor_id)[names(by_donor)]),
    row.names = names(by_donor))
by_status <- tapply(by_donor, status[names(by_donor)], sum)
by_status
```

Of the sampled basal cells of the donors with permuted status 0,
`r by_status[["0"]]` have a count of one of the two genes, against
`r by_status[["1"]]` of the cells of the donors with status 1. A call under a
shuffled status is no evidence of an effect of smoking. It need not be noise,
though: a shuffled status can happen to divide the donors by something that
does differ between them, as the share of dividing cells among the ten cells
sampled from each donor may here. The model then finds a difference that is
there, and what would be wrong is to read it as an effect of the status.

## What the check shows

* In `r sum(permutations$calls == 0)` of the 20 permuted labellings the
  pipeline calls nothing, and between
  `r min(permutations$p_below_0.05[permutations$calls == 0])` and
  `r max(permutations$p_below_0.05[permutations$calls == 0])` of their
  p-values are below 0.05. A test that called many genes for most labellings
  would be suspect; that is the failure this check can find.
* Calls come together, because genes are correlated. The number of calls in
  one labelling therefore says little, and the number of labellings with any
  call is the better summary.
* Twenty labellings of 420 do not estimate an error rate, and 420 would not
  either: the labellings overlap with the observed one (`same_label`), and
  they are few.
* The check assumes that donors could have had each other's status. For an
  exposure that was not assigned at random this does not hold. Smokers and
  never smokers differ in more than smoking, and a permutation removes those
  differences from the comparison along with the exposure.

# Two backends on the same data

`method = "voom_dream"` fits another model to the same pseudobulk counts.
Agreement between backends does not show that either is right; it shows how
much of a result depends on the choice.

```{r backends, eval=has("variancePartition")}
voom <- run_sc_exwas(x, exposure = "smoking", covariates = "chemistry_v3",
    method = "voom_dream", celltypes = "Basal")
common <- intersect(observed$gene, voom$gene)
c(edgeR = nrow(observed), voom_dream = nrow(voom), both = length(common))
edger_common <- observed[match(common, observed$gene), ]
voom_common <- voom[match(common, voom$gene), ]
cor(edger_common$log2FC, voom_common$log2FC)
table(edgeR = edger_common$padj_global < 0.05,
    voom_dream = voom_common$padj_global < 0.05)
```

The backends do not test the same genes, because each has its own expression
filter, so their `padj_global` values are adjusted over families of different
sizes. The estimates of the genes that both test are strongly correlated but
not equal, as the figure shows; the calls, which sit at the edge of a
threshold, need not agree.

```{r backend-plot, eval=has("variancePartition"), fig.width=4, fig.height=4}
#| fig.cap: >-
#|   Log2 fold changes of the genes tested by both backends in basal cells.
plot(edger_common$log2FC, voom_common$log2FC, pch = 16, cex = 0.4,
    col = "grey40", xlab = "edgeR log2FC", ylab = "voom-dream log2FC")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
```

# Two adjustments of the p-values

`run_sc_exwas()` returns `padj`, adjusted within each cell type, and
`padj_global`, adjusted once over all tested genes and cell types.

```{r multiplicity}
full <- run_sc_exwas(x, exposure = "smoking", covariates = "chemistry_v3")
table(celltype = full$celltype, padj = full$padj < 0.05,
    padj_global = full$padj_global < 0.05)
```

The two are answers to different questions. `padj` controls the false
discovery rate among the calls of one cell type, taken alone. `padj_global`
controls it among all calls of the analysis, which is what a list of calls
across cell types needs. Neither is uniformly the stricter one: a gene can
pass the threshold of the larger family without passing that of its own cell
type, when other cell types contribute many small p-values.

# How many donors

`estimate_power()` approximates the power of a pseudobulk test for one gene in
one cell type at a Bonferroni level for the number of tests, from the number
of donors, the log2 fold change per unit of the exposure, the standard
deviation of the exposure, the dispersion and the mean pseudobulk count. It
treats the dispersion as known and is optimistic for small numbers of donors.
The Bonferroni level is stricter than the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment behind
`padj_global`, so the table is not the power to be called in the analysis
above.

The effect is per unit of the exposure, so the spread of the exposure matters
as much as the size of the effect. A status that half of the donors have, as
the smoking status here, has a standard deviation of 0.5; the default of
`exposure_sd` is 1, which suits an exposure that was standardised. The call
asks for the power to find a doubling of expression between two groups of
equal size (`effect_size = 1`) at the Bonferroni level for as many tests as
the analysis above made:

```{r power}
estimate_power(n_donors = c(12, 24, 48, 96), effect_size = 1,
    exposure_sd = 0.5, n_genes = nrow(full), n_celltypes = 1,
    dispersion = 0.1, base_mean = 100)
```

`n_genes` times `n_celltypes` is the number of tests; here all tests of the
three cell types are given as one number.

Donors, not cells, are the units: more cells per donor raise the pseudobulk
count, which enters through `base_mean`, but they do not add to `n_donors`.
